Definition: Whether the country has an operational Internet Exchange Point (IXP) and its maturity. IXPs enable local internet traffic to be exchanged domestically rather than being routed internationally, reducing latency, costs, and dependence on foreign infrastructure. Critical for local digital ecosystem development.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original score was 0/Unknown with no source. A light check found Mali's IXP listed in the Packet Clearing House directory, so the row was moved to full verification. MLIX (Mali Internet Exchange), established February 2018 and managed by telecoms regulator AMRTP, is confirmed active in both the PCH directory and PeeringDB, which lists 5 peering participants and a total capacity of 5G — a single, small-scale IXP with limited participation.
revised_comments: Mali operates a single Internet Exchange Point, MLIX, established in Bamako in February 2018 and managed by the telecommunications regulator AMRTP. PeeringDB records five participating networks with a combined capacity of 5G, indicating limited participation typical of an early-stage exchange.

Definition: The country's overall cybersecurity preparedness, based on the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI). Covers legal measures, technical measures, organisational measures, capacity development, and cooperation. Essential for trust in stored data and digital services.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original score was 0/Unknown with no source. A light check surfaced ITU Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI) data for Mali, so the row was moved to full verification. Mali scored 29.47/100 in the ITU GCI 2024 (up from 10.14 in 2020), placing it in Tier 4 of 5. The pillar breakdown (legal 12.36/20, technical 4.56/20, organisational 2.90/20, capacity development 0.79/20, cooperation 8.87/20) is corroborated by a We Are Tech Africa report citing the same ITU release.
revised_comments: Mali scored 29.47 out of 100 on the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024, placing it in the fourth of five tiers, with relative strength in legal measures but weak organisational and capacity-development measures. A national cybersecurity strategy for 2026-2030 was approved by the Council of Ministers in December 2025 to address these gaps.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original score was 0/Unknown with no source. A light check surfaced Mali's 2013 Personal Data Protection Act, so the row was moved to full verification. That law (as amended in 2017) imposes an adequacy-based restriction on cross-border transfers of personal data but does not itself mandate that data be physically stored within Mali — a data-transfer control rather than a data localisation requirement as the variable defines it. Separately, in January 2026 Mali inaugurated a Tier III government data centre explicitly intended to repatriate public-sector data previously hosted abroad, signalling a clear policy direction toward data sovereignty, but this is an infrastructure/policy initiative rather than a codified cross-sector legal requirement. Given the mismatch between a transfer-restriction law and a true localisation mandate, and the absence of a dedicated localisation statute, this is flagged for human review rather than assigning a code that could overstate or understate the legal position.
revised_comments: Mali's Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 2013-015, amended 2017) restricts cross-border transfers of personal data to countries deemed to offer adequate protection, but does not impose a general legal requirement that data be stored within national borders. In January 2026 the government inaugurated a Tier III data centre in Bamako intended to host government platforms and repatriate state data previously held abroad, signalling a policy commitment to digital sovereignty that has not yet been codified into a data localisation law.

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original score was 0/Unknown with no source. A light check surfaced current electricity tariff data for Mali, so the row was moved to full verification. Residential electricity costs approximately USD 0.22-0.23/kWh (2025), among the highest in Africa alongside Sierra Leone and Burkina Faso, against a GNI per capita of roughly USD 1,010-1,030 (2023-24). Converting this to the affordability scale requires a defined 'basic service' consumption benchmark (e.g. the World Bank Multi-Tier Framework's 30-50 kWh/month subsistence level), and no current, Mali-specific study computing the resulting share of income was found (the closest World Bank analysis using this methodology dates from 2016 and pre-2013 survey data). Depending on the consumption assumption used, the estimated share of GNI per capita ranges from roughly 8% to 14%, straddling the 'Expensive' and 'Very Expensive' bands, so this is flagged for human review rather than guessed.
revised_comments: Residential electricity in Mali costs approximately USD 0.22-0.23 per kWh (2025), among the highest rates in the West Africa region, reflecting a generation mix dominated by imported fossil fuels. Against a GNI per capita of around USD 1,010-1,030, this represents a significant cost burden for basic household consumption, though no current study precisely quantifies electricity's share of household income for Mali.

Definition: The scale and quality of tertiary-level ICT and STEM education programmes available in the country, based on the number and quality of institutions offering ICT degrees, computer science programmes, and engineering courses relative to the population.
Value Name: Very limited (<2 institutions with ICT programmes)
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The original score of 1 (Very limited, <2 institutions) rested on a 2007 infoDev/World Bank survey report describing Mali's education-ICT context nearly two decades ago; that source, fetched and read, does not support a current assessment and does not itself even discuss the number of ICT/CS-specific tertiary programmes. Verification found several current institutions offering dedicated computer science/IT programmes: the public Université des Sciences, des Techniques et des Technologies de Bamako (USTTB), whose Institut des Sciences Appliquées offers applied-sciences/electronics programmes and whose Faculté des Sciences et Techniques covers science and technology degrees; the private Université du Sahel, which has a dedicated Faculté d'Informatique offering licence-level computer science degrees; the University of Social Sciences and Management of Bamako (USSGB), offering Licence and Master's degrees in IT management, cybersecurity and cloud computing; and ISFIC, a private higher-education institute founded in 1999 specialising in IT and digital-technology training. This constitutes several active institutions with ICT/CS programmes, inconsistent with the original 'very limited (<2 institutions)' score. No verified enrolment data was found, so 'Moderate' rather than 'Good/Strong' is used.
revised_comments: Mali has several tertiary institutions offering dedicated computer science and ICT programmes, including the public Université des Sciences, des Techniques et des Technologies de Bamako (with its Institut des Sciences Appliquées and Faculté des Sciences et Techniques), the private Université du Sahel's Faculté d'Informatique, the University of Social Sciences and Management of Bamako's IT management and cybersecurity degrees, and the private ISFIC institute. Enrolment scale across these institutions is not precisely documented, but the number and diversity of active programmes indicate a moderate and growing tertiary ICT education base.
